title: Modelling Co‐Occurrence of Marine Pelagic Species in the Northern Humboldt Current System
content:
ABSTRACT

The northern Humboldt Current System (nHCS) is among the most productive marine ecosystems worldwide, supporting highly dynamic pelagic communities. However, the relative contributions of environmental conditions, spatial processes and species associations to community organization have not been quantified together. We asked to what extent community structure is dominated by environmental variables versus residual (biotic or abiotic) dependencies. We fitted year-specific Joint Species Distribution Models (JSDMs) to acoustic data for six pelagic taxa from summer surveys collected by the Instituto del Mar del Perú (IMARPE) between 2013 and 2019. We modelled the community abundance matrix using a two-part hurdle approach to account for zero inflation in the acoustic data, allowing the joint analysing of species occurrence and abundance patterns in relation to environmental and spatial drivers. Occurrence models showed good predictive performance (mean cross-validated AUC = 0.83), whereas abundance models had low explanatory power (mean R2$$ {R}^2 $$ = 0.07). Environmental covariates, led by distance to the shelf break, dissolved oxygen and sea surface temperature, jointly accounted for 69%–83% of the explained variance in occurrence, versus 17%–31% for the spatial random effect. Significant residual species associations were observed only in occurrence models and were weaker or absent in years of strong environmental anomalies. Environmental filtering is therefore the primary organising mechanism of pelagic community structure in the nHCS, with spatial and biotic processes modulating it among years. For ecosystem-based management, these results support monitoring and managing co-occurrence of pelagic taxa jointly, using oxygen and temperature conditions as early indicators of community reorganization under ENSO and climate variability.
